https://www.dw.com/en/russia-wants-black.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OM9P Zaporizhzia in eastern Ukraine came under renewed attack overnight Image: REUTERS Advertisement Russia is stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in a bid to cut electricity and heating in the country as winter approaches, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday. His remarks come as Moscow intensifies its attacks on civilian targets in the capital, Kyiv, and elsewhere, with key observers saying its objective is to render the country virtually unlivable. Overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia killed a 64-year-old man Image: Daria Nazarova/AFP What did Zelenskyy say? In a post on social media platform X, Zelenskyy said Russia had just carried out one of its biggest attacks on Ukraine 's energy sector since it began its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022. "More than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine," he wrote. "Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved," he added. Zelenskyy said that Russia was planning to leave Ukrainian citizens in the cold this winter. "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine — right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating," he wrote, calling on allies to put pressure on Moscow to stop this happening. He said Russia had "expanded ‌its campaign ​against the energy system" and was trying "to stretch ⁠Ukraine's ​reserves ​and repair ​capacity as ‌thinly as possible." ​ Russia claims multiple infrastructure attacks The Russian Defense Ministry, for its part, said on Saturday that its forces had attacked several infrastructure targets in Ukraine overnight. Among those named was an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr. However, it also said Ukraine's largest steelworks, in the city of Kryvyi Rih, had been hit, saying the facility supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex. It said another steel plant in ​Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front ​line, had also been struck. Ukrainian authorities have also said that one person — an ambulance driver — was killed ​and ‌19 others injured, including a child, in a Russian airstrike on Kherson in southern Ukraine. Russian state news ​agency TASS has also reported the death of one woman as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region that also injured a man. Russia's overnight attacks hit numerous civilian sites Image: REUTERS Trump's sanctions waiver a boost for Putin: Zelenskyy Meanwhile, Zelenskyy also reacted to US President Donald Trump's decision to waive a package of new sanctions on Moscow, saying the move would only encourage Russian leader Vladimir Putin . "A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelenskyy said. On Friday, Trump signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect. The waiver has been hailed by a Russian presidential envoy as a "historic moment." "The Trump administration's suspension of the [Lindsey] Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said on social media. Dmitriev said the act, named for the late US senator who sponsored the bill , "would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets." Trump's move came as he increasingly criticizes Zelenskyy, fueling speculation that the US leader is siding with Moscow in the conflict. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm98.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L) By Steve Rosenberg Russia Editor ,Â Reporting from Moscow Published 1 hour ago After two days of diplomacy â in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg â is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending? "Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives. In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting. But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow. The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level. In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..." Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war Published 3 hours ago Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism Published 1 day ago US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin Published 30 minutes ago For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks. Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv". The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard. "In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov. Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace. "I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said, "but things are moving in that direction." All rather vague. It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war. He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain. He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission. He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken hold In recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky. That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader. "Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says. "Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?" "Of course!" A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent. But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit. Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe. "Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China." After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.
